rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.2 and 3; three-year field experiment (2012-2014) at Shihezi, Xinjiang, with five fertilizer levels and three drip irrigation levels in a randomized factorial design, reporting LAI, dry matter, seed cotton yield, WUE, PFP and economic benefits.
rows.notes: All fifteen treatments are drip-fertigated under plastic mulch; the study varies water amount (0.6-1.0 ETc) and N-P2O5-K2O rate, with no non-drip comparison. It therefore shows how yield, WUE and PFP respond to water and fertilizer rates under drip (max yield at 1.0 ETc with 300-120-60 kg/ha; regression optima in Tables 5-6), not that drip itself improves yield, quality or water/fertilizer productivity relative to another irrigation method. Fiber quality was not measured. Standard errors are given for yield (Fig. 3) but do not count since Q2 is no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.2 and 3.3; own three-year field experiment reporting WUE (Table 3) and irrigation amounts (Table 1) for drip-irrigated cotton treatments.
rows.notes: The study reports WUE and irrigation amounts only among drip treatments differing in water and fertilizer rates; it has no comparison with another irrigation method, so it does not establish that drip saves water or is high-efficiency relative to alternatives. It actually finds WUE lowest under full drip irrigation and that reduced irrigation cut economic benefits, noting farmers' weak willingness to save water (Section 3.4). Evidence is about irrigation amount and fertilizer coupling under drip, not about drip as a technology.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a water x fertilizer rate experiment entirely under mulched drip fertigation on one sandy loam site with one crop; it contains no drip-versus-other-method contrast, so it cannot support claims about drip per se for either crop production or water conservation.
